Eswatini ANC Guidelines: re-extracted tables, boxes and flowcharts

Every table, highlighted box and flowchart in the ANC guidelines, read from the PDF page image by Claude: merged cells, section rows and footnotes kept for tables; branches, combined conditions and line breaks kept for flowcharts, with their captions and printed notes folded in. Compare each with the page on the left. "Points to check in the source" lists problems in the guideline itself. The "what the model receives" version fills merged cells in, shows a long note that spans every row once, and attaches footnotes. The embedding text is split into parts under 512 tokens that all return the whole table.

Eight ANC contacts schedule: 1st contact 8-12 weeks, then 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks

A new model with eight scheduled contacts is adopted (WHO 2016), replacing focused ANC (4 visits), to reduce perinatal mortality and improve women's experience of care.

ContactRecommended schedule
1st contactAs soon as the woman suspects she is pregnant; during the first trimester (preferably 8–12 weeks)
2nd scheduled contact20 weeks
3rd scheduled contact26 weeks
4th scheduled contact30 weeks
5th scheduled contact34 weeks
6th scheduled contact36 weeks
7th scheduled contact38 weeks
8th scheduled contact40 weeks

Points to check in the source:
  • The PDF prints each contact as a rotated landscape table with no text layer; cells were transcribed from the page images.
  • Several cells are printed twice (contact 3, 4 and 5 preventive measures, clinical practices, management and 'Others'), and on contact 5 text from the maternal-assessment and counselling cells overflows into the preventive-measures and clinical-practices cells. Cleaned up here; the order of the overflow text was inferred.
  • The 'Cadres' row on p.22 has six columns in the first block and five in the second; mapped to the 11 columns in printed order, so the mapping should be checked.
  • Calcium and IFA are listed at every contact but doses are not given in this table.

NB: 1. All cadres will be expected to provide IEC; depending on the roster, all midwives will be expected to provide individual counselling. 2. Health promotion will be done for community engagement. 3. Complete the ANC card, enter information into the register and give the card to the pregnant woman. 4. ANC services are offered at clinic, PHU and health centre. 5. Referral for complications to the next level.

IPV – intimate partner violence; HTSP – healthy timing and spacing of pregnancy; IYCF – infant and young child feeding; EIMC – early infant male circumcision; ASB – asymptomatic bacteriuria; IFA – iron and folic acid; SFH – symphysis-fundal height; FHR – foetal heart rate.

Eswatini ANC Guidelines | 2.0 ANC Contact Schedule > 2.2 Essential Package of ANC Interventions (page 14)

Essential package of ANC interventions at each of the 8 contacts: maternal and foetal assessment, counselling topics, point-of-care tests, lab investigations, ultrasound, preventive measures (IFA, calcium, deworming, PrEP), clinical practices, management, and cadres (part 1 of 9).
Contact 1 at 8–12 weeks: Maternal assessment: Comprehensive history taking; clinical estimation of gestational age; examination head to toe; TB screening; screening for IPV; Foetal assessment: —; Counselling topics (information, education and counselling): Nutrition; diet; physical activity, rest, HIV test and partner testing, adherence to medicines prescribed; danger signs, emergency preparedness, early stimulation of the baby, VMMC counselling, condom usage; avoid: caffeine intake, alcohol/tobacco/substance abuse; Point-of-care tests: HIV, syphilis, Hep B, urine dipstick, malaria, Hb; Lab investigations: Blood group and Rhesus; full blood count; check for ASB (Gram stain or culture); viral load, CD4 count; Hep B; Radiological tests: Ultrasound; Preventive measures: Iron and folic acid, calcium, TT/Td; combination prevention (PrEP, condom, VMMC for men); prophylaxis as needed; Essential good clinical practices: Weight, height, BP, MUAC, male involvement, STI screening; Treat / manage: Common physiological disorders; STIs; complications of early pregnancy; ART; refer as per client's needs; Others: Complete ANC card and give to woman; fill ANC register/CMIS.

2.2 Essential package of ANC interventions

Although the country has never had comprehensive ANC guidelines, there has been a set of interventions on good clinical practice that continue to be implemented as part of the essential ANC package of interventions. These interventions shall be maintained and aligned to the recommended schedule of ANC contacts. The essential package of ANC interventions will be as follows:

3.0 Providing ANC Services

ANC services can start as soon as the woman misses a period and suspects that she is pregnant. The ANC services that are provided must be in line with the ANC service package outlined in this guideline.

Preventive measures in ANC by risk condition: iron/folate for anaemia (60 mg iron + 400 mcg folic acid daily), calcium 1500 mg for pre-eclampsia, mebendazole 500 mg, malaria, HIV testing and ART, hepatitis B testing

Risk conditionAssess, check, recordTreat and adviseScheduled contact
Iron deficiency anaemiaCheck the woman's supply of the prescribed dose of iron/folate and whether she is taking them regularly as advised. Ask about diet.Start iron/folate supplements at the first contact. Give 3 months' supply of daily iron/folate (1 tablet = 60 mg iron + 400 mcg folic acid), to be taken daily by all pregnant women to prevent anaemia. Refill the supply of iron/folate at subsequent contacts.<br/>Counsel on adherence to prevent anaemia.<br/>Counsel on correct and consistent use, management of side effects, and appropriate iron-rich food intake including food preparation.All scheduled contacts
Pre-eclampsiaAll women are at risk of pre-eclampsia. Check the woman's supply of calcium tablets at each contact.Dispense 1500 mg of elemental calcium. Give 1500 mg to every pregnant woman at risk of developing pre-eclampsia (multiple pregnancy, obesity, family history of pre-eclampsia, diabetes) from 20 weeks until delivery.All scheduled contacts
Intestinal wormsCheck when the woman last received a dose of mebendazole (if within the previous 6 months, wait until 6 months have passed).Give mebendazole (500 mg) once during the second or third trimester of pregnancy to every woman.Contact 2 at 20 weeks
MalariaCheck when the last dose of an antimalarial was given.Counsel on use of bed nets.<br/>Perform RDT if she has malaria symptoms and treat if positive.All contacts
HIVCheck knowledge of HIV status and partner's status.Counsel and offer HIV testing to HIV-negative women and those of unknown HIV status. If negative, retest as per schedule; encourage partner HIV testing. If positive and not on treatment, start ART (see National HIV integrated guidelines, PMTCT section).<br/>Provide adherence and psychosocial support; if on ART provide support; encourage and emphasise the use of condoms and encourage VMMC.All scheduled contacts
Hepatitis BCheck knowledge about hepatitis; history of blood transfusion, jaundice, contact/exposure to hepatitis B.Test for hepatitis B; if positive, counsel and refer to the next level of care. If negative, counsel and repeat when the next HIV/syphilis screening is done.1st contact

Td (tetanus-diphtheria) vaccination in pregnancy by prior TTCV doses: unknown/none, 3 or 4 childhood doses, later boosters – doses needed and intervals

PDF page 27 · anc-fig-td-vaccination · replaces anc-0055, anc-0056
Check: {"new_not_in_pdf_text": ["1", "2", "3", "4", "6"], "new_not_in_old_chunks": [], "old_not_in_new": []} (compared with the PDF text layer and the old chunks)

PDF page

New: flowchart

If a pregnant woman received:
- No TTCV doses or unknown vaccination status → she will need: (a) 1 Td dose as early as possible; (b) 1 Td dose at least 4 weeks later; (c) 1 Td dose at least 6 months later; (d) 1 Td dose at least 1 year later; (e) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (to obtain long-term protection).
- Only 3 TTCV doses in childhood → (a) 1 Td dose at the first ANC visit; (b) another Td dose 4 weeks later (to be protected for that pregnancy); (c) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (long-term protection).
- 4 TTCV doses in childhood → (a) 1 Td dose at that visit (to be protected for that pregnancy); (b) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (long-term protection).
- 3 TTCV doses in childhood and 1 Td or 1 DT dose later → (a) 1 Td dose at that visit (to be protected for that pregnancy); (b) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (long-term protection).
- 4 TTCV doses in childhood and 1 Td dose later → 1 Td dose at that contact (no further doses required).
- 4 TTCV doses and 2 Td boosters → no vaccination; the woman is fully protected.
(TTCV = tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine.)

New: what the model receives

Td (tetanus-diphtheria) vaccination in pregnancy by prior TTCV doses: unknown/none, 3 or 4 childhood doses, later boosters – doses needed and intervals

If a pregnant woman received:

- No TTCV doses or unknown vaccination status → she will need: (a) 1 Td dose as early as possible; (b) 1 Td dose at least 4 weeks later; (c) 1 Td dose at least 6 months later; (d) 1 Td dose at least 1 year later; (e) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (to obtain long-term protection).

- Only 3 TTCV doses in childhood → (a) 1 Td dose at the first ANC visit; (b) another Td dose 4 weeks later (to be protected for that pregnancy); (c) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (long-term protection).

- 4 TTCV doses in childhood → (a) 1 Td dose at that visit (to be protected for that pregnancy); (b) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (long-term protection).

- 3 TTCV doses in childhood and 1 Td or 1 DT dose later → (a) 1 Td dose at that visit (to be protected for that pregnancy); (b) 1 more Td dose at least 1 year later (long-term protection).

- 4 TTCV doses in childhood and 1 Td dose later → 1 Td dose at that contact (no further doses required).

- 4 TTCV doses and 2 Td boosters → no vaccination; the woman is fully protected.

(TTCV = tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine.)

Ectopic pregnancy: symptoms (amenorrhoea, unilateral lower abdominal pain, spotting, shoulder tip pain, collapse), signs, and emergency management (IV lines, urgent referral)

Ectopic pregnancy is implantation of the pregnancy outside the uterine cavity.

SymptomsSignsManagement
- Often asymptomatic (unsure of dates)
- Amenorrhoea (usually 6–8 weeks)
- Lower abdominal pain (classically unilateral)
- Vaginal bleeding (usually spotting and brown in colour)
- Diarrhoea and vomiting should not be ignored
- Dizziness and light-headedness
- Shoulder tip pain (diaphragmatic irritation – haemoperitoneum)
- Collapse (if ruptured)		- Often no specific signs
- Uterus usually normal size
- Cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness occasionally
- Adnexal mass very rare
- Confusion and restlessness
(Suspect ectopic pregnancy in any woman of reproductive age with a history of amenorrhoea and unilateral lower abdominal pain, tachycardia, dizziness, fainting.)		- Vital signs: pulse, blood pressure; do pregnancy test and haemoglobin. NOTE: tachycardia should be taken seriously even in a stable-looking patient.
- Insert 2 large-bore IV lines
- Run normal saline or Ringer's lactate
- Refer urgently to hospital
- Ultrasound scan must be done. This is an emergency and must be managed immediately!

New: what the model receives

Antepartum haemorrhage: abruptio placentae vs placenta praevia vs ruptured uterus – signs and symptoms; general emergency management (ABC, IV lines, no digital vaginal examination, refer)

APH is bleeding from or into the genital tract from 28 weeks of pregnancy until before delivery of the baby. Any bleeding in a pregnant woman should be taken seriously. Spotting; minor haemorrhage <50 ml that has settled; major haemorrhage 50–1000 ml with no signs of shock; massive haemorrhage >1000 ml and/or signs of clinical shock.

Probable diagnosisSigns and symptoms
Abruptio placentae- Vaginal bleeding
- Intermittent or constant abdominal pain
- Shock
- Tender, tense uterus
- Decreased or absent fetal movement
- Fetal distress or absent fetal heart sounds
Placenta praevia- Vaginal bleeding (painless, bright red), may be precipitated by intercourse
- Shock
- Relaxed uterus
- Fetal presentation not in the pelvis; malpresentation; lower uterine pole feels empty
- Normal fetal condition
Ruptured uterus- Vaginal or intra-abdominal bleeding
- Severe abdominal pain (may decrease after rupture)
- Shock
- Abdominal distension or free fluid
- Abnormal uterine contour
- Tender abdomen
- Easily palpable fetal parts
- Absent fetal movement and fetal heart sounds
- Rapid maternal pulse

Management (applies to every row): General management:
Shout for help! (Inyandzaleyo!)
- Follow A, B, C: airway clear, breathing, circulation.
- Assess the haemodynamic status of the patient.
- Vital signs: pulse, blood pressure; do urgent ward Hb.
- NOTE: tachycardia should be taken seriously even in a stable-looking patient; also confusion and restlessness.
- Resuscitate as appropriate: insert 2 large IV lines; correct hypovolaemia using normal saline or Ringer's lactate; strict fluid balance chart, insert Foley's catheter, monitor input and output; if available give oxygen 4–6 L per minute by face mask; blood grouping and cross-match, FBC.
Refer the patient to hospital as soon as possible.
NOTE: DO NOT PERFORM DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION UNTIL PLACENTA PRAEVIA IS RULED OUT.

(Inyandzaleyo!)<br/>- Follow A, B, C: airway clear, breathing, circulation.<br/>- Assess the haemodynamic status of the patient.<br/>- Vital signs: pulse, blood pressure; do urgent ward Hb.<br/>- NOTE: tachycardia should be taken seriously even in a stable-looking patient; also confusion and restlessness.<br/>- Resuscitate as appropriate: insert 2 large IV lines; correct hypovolaemia using normal saline or Ringer's lactate; strict fluid balance chart, insert Foley's catheter, monitor input and output; if available give oxygen 4–6 L per minute by face mask; blood grouping and cross-match, FBC.<br/>Refer the patient to hospital as soon as possible.<br/>NOTE: DO NOT PERFORM DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION UNTIL PLACENTA PRAEVIA IS RULED OUT.

*6.3.3 Diagnosis of Antepartum haemorrhage*

Probable diagnosisSigns and symptomsManagement
Abruptio placenta• Vaginal Bleeding
• Intermittent or constant abdominal pain
• Shock
• Tender tense uterus
• Decreased or absent fetal movement
• Fetal distress or absent fetal sounds		General management
*Shout for help!!!! (Inyandzaleyo!!!!)*
• Follow A, B, C:
o Airways clear
o Breathing
o Circulation
• Assess the hemodynamics status of the patient.
• Vital signs: pulse, blood pressure and do urgent ward HB.
• NOTE: Tachycardia should be taken seriously even in a stable looking patient, confusion and restlessness.
• Resuscitate the patient as appropriate
o Insert 2 large IV lines.
o Correct hypovolaemia using normal saline or Ringer’s Lactate
o Strict fluid balance chart. Insert Foleys catheter. Monitor input and output.
o If available give oxygen 4 to 6 L per minute to the mother by facemask.
o Blood grouping and cross match, FBC.
Refer the patient to hospital as soon as possible.
NOTE: DO NOT PERFORM DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION UNTIL PLACENTA PRAEVIA IS RULED OUT.
Placenta praevia• Vaginal bleeding (painless and bright red in colour) may be precipitated by intercourse
• Shock
• Relaxed uterus
• Fetal presentation not in the pelvis; malpresentation, lower uterine pole feels empty
Normal fetal condition
Probable diagnosisSigns and symptomsManagement
Ruptured uterus• Vaginal or intra-abdominal bleeding
• Severe abdominal pain (may decreased after rupture)
• Shock
• Abdominal distension or free fluid
• Abdominal uterine contour
• Tender abdomen
• Easily palpable fetal parts
• Absent fetal movement and fetal heart sounds
• Rapid maternal pulse

Eclampsia: risk factors, symptoms and emergency management of convulsions (left lateral, airway, oxygen, magnesium sulphate, urgent referral)
Risk factorsSymptomsManagement
- 1st pregnancy<br/>- Age >40 years<br/>- Overweight (BMI >35 at 1st ANC visit)<br/>- Family history of PIH / pre-eclampsia<br/>- Multiple pregnancy<br/>- Last pregnancy >10 years ago<br/>- Chronic kidney disease<br/>- Diabetes mellitus<br/>- Autoimmune diseases<br/>- Race – black<br/>- Chronic hypertension- May be asymptomatic<br/>- Headache not relieved by simple analgesia<br/>- Altered mental state<br/>- Blindness<br/>- Shortness of breath<br/>- Blurred vision or flashing<br/>- Epigastric / right upper quadrant abdominal pain<br/>- Rapid swelling of face, hands and feet<br/>- Non-specific complaints of being unwell<br/>- Convulsions- Urgently refer the patient to the nearest hospital.<br/>- Give a pre-referral loading dose of magnesium sulphate 4 g IM.<br/>- For a patient with convulsions: do not leave the patient alone; shout for assistance, state 'Eclampsia'; turn the patient to the left lateral position; ensure the airway is clear and the patient is breathing; protect the patient from falling/injury; do not place anything in the mouth; oxygen by mask at 4–6 L per minute; when the convulsion ends, start IV; take vital signs.<br/>- At the hospital, stabilise the patient and deliver by the safest, fastest route; manage eclampsia as per guidelines.

Eclampsia: risk factors, symptoms and emergency management of convulsions (left lateral, airway, oxygen, magnesium sulphate, urgent referral)

Eclampsia: seizures that cannot be attributed to other causes in a woman with pre-eclampsia.

Risk factorsSymptomsManagement
- 1st pregnancy
- Age >40 years
- Overweight (BMI >35 at 1st ANC visit)
- Family history of PIH / pre-eclampsia
- Multiple pregnancy
- Last pregnancy >10 years ago
- Chronic kidney disease
- Diabetes mellitus
- Autoimmune diseases
- Race – black
- Chronic hypertension		- May be asymptomatic
- Headache not relieved by simple analgesia
- Altered mental state
- Blindness
- Shortness of breath
- Blurred vision or flashing
- Epigastric / right upper quadrant abdominal pain
- Rapid swelling of face, hands and feet
- Non-specific complaints of being unwell
- Convulsions		- Urgently refer the patient to the nearest hospital.
- Give a pre-referral loading dose of magnesium sulphate 4 g IM.
- For a patient with convulsions: do not leave the patient alone; shout for assistance, state 'Eclampsia'; turn the patient to the left lateral position; ensure the airway is clear and the patient is breathing; protect the patient from falling/injury; do not place anything in the mouth; oxygen by mask at 4–6 L per minute; when the convulsion ends, start IV; take vital signs.
- At the hospital, stabilise the patient and deliver by the safest, fastest route; manage eclampsia as per guidelines.

Risk factors:Symptoms:Management
• 1st pregnancy• May be asymptomatic• Urgently refer the patient to the nearest hospital

6.6 Premature rupture of membranes

*6.6.1 Definition*

* Premature rupture of membranes (PROM) is the drainage of amniotic fluid through the cervical canal before the onset of uterine contractions.

* PROM may be Pre-term (before 37 weeks of gestation) or at-Term (post 37 weeks of gestation).

Points to check in the source:
  • Pre-referral magnesium sulphate is given as '4 g IM'. The WHO IM regimen is 4 g IV plus 10 g IM (5 g in each buttock), or 10 g IM where IV is not possible; 4 g IM alone is below standard loading doses. Clinician to confirm.
  • 'Mild' pre-eclampsia still uses the older '30/15 mmHg rise' criterion, which is no longer used to define hypertension in pregnancy.

CategorySigns and symptomsManagement
Mild pre-eclampsia- BP ≥140/90 on ≥2 occasions measured at least 4 hours apart, without evidence of end-organ damage, in women with previously normal BP before 20 weeks' gestation<br/>OR<br/>- An increase in systolic BP by 30 mmHg or diastolic BP by 15 mmHgRefer the client to the regional referral hospital (if at the clinic, PHU). Pre-eclampsia is new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks' gestation with significant proteinuria, with or without oedema; it can present as late as 4–6 weeks postpartum.

CategorySigns and symptomsManagement
Mild pre-eclampsia- BP ≥140/90 on ≥2 occasions measured at least 4 hours apart, without evidence of end-organ damage, in women with previously normal BP before 20 weeks' gestation
OR
- An increase in systolic BP by 30 mmHg or diastolic BP by 15 mmHg		Refer the client to the regional referral hospital (if at the clinic, PHU). At the hospital, manage as per guidelines.
Severe pre-eclampsia: any 1 of the following in the presence of pre-eclampsia- SBP ≥160 mmHg or DBP ≥110 mmHg
- Proteinuria >5 g in a 24-hour urine collection or 3+ on dipstick
- Pulmonary oedema / cyanosis
- Urine output <30 ml/hr (oliguria)
- Persistent headaches
- Blurred vision
- Epigastric pain ± impaired liver function
- Oligohydramnios
- Decreased fetal growth
- Placental abruption
- Thrombocytopenia		Refer the client to the regional referral hospital (if at the clinic, PHU). Give a pre-referral loading dose of magnesium sulphate 4 g IM if at the clinic or PHU. At the hospital, manage as per guidelines.

Premature rupture of membranes (PROM) and preterm PROM (PPROM): assessment, clinic management (no digital vaginal exam, refer), hospital management by gestation (steroids betamethasone/dexamethasone, antibiotics erythromycin/amoxicillin, induction)
DiagnosisAssessmentGeneral management (clinic, PHU)Management at health centre / hospital
Premature rupture of membranes (PROM)- Verify the patient's estimated due date; this will be needed for management decisions.<br/>- Vital signs: pulse, blood pressure and temperature 4-hourly.<br/>- Do urine dipstick.<br/>- Check fetal heart rate.- DO NOT perform digital vaginal examination.<br/>- Refer to health centre or hospital.- If term, this may indicate onset of labour.<br/>- Assess for other signs of labour.<br/>- Perform a sterile speculum examination to assess whether the cervix is open.<br/>- Give antibiotics if prolonged rupture of membranes.<br/>- Allow to deliver if in labour.
Preterm PROM (PPROM)- Assess as indicated in PROM.<br/>- Ultrasound at least twice a day.<br/>- Consider weekly maternal FBC.- DO NOT perform digital vaginal examination.<br/>- Refer to health centre or hospital.If rupture is:<br/>- Before 28 weeks: observe vital signs; initiate the process of evacuation by stimulation after counselling the mother and significant others about the risks.<br/>- Before 34 weeks (28–33 weeks): administer steroids – intramuscular betamethasone 12 mg every 12 hours for 24 hours, OR intramuscular dexamethasone.<br/>- Regularly inspect the sanitary pad for the amount, colour and odour of the amniotic fluid.<br/>- Strict bed rest.<br/>- Oral erythromycin and amoxicillin (500 mg PO 6-hourly) should be given for 10 days following the diagnosis of PPROM.
PPROM >34 and <37 weeks, and PROM >37 weeksAssess as indicated in PROM.Refer to hospital (transfer is preferable while the baby is in utero).- Give antibiotic prophylaxis within 8 hours.<br/>- Give steroids before 37 weeks.<br/>- If no evidence of fetal distress, leave the patient for up to 24 hours.<br/>- If the patient does not go into labour within 24 hours, induce.<br/>- Monitor labour normally.

Premature rupture of membranes (PROM) and preterm PROM (PPROM): assessment, clinic management (no digital vaginal exam, refer), hospital management by gestation (steroids betamethasone/dexamethasone, antibiotics erythromycin/amoxicillin, induction)

PROM is drainage of amniotic fluid through the cervical canal before the onset of uterine contractions; it may be preterm (before 37 weeks) or at term (after 37 weeks).

DiagnosisAssessmentGeneral management (clinic, PHU)Management at health centre / hospital
Premature rupture of membranes (PROM)- Verify the patient's estimated due date; this will be needed for management decisions.
- Vital signs: pulse, blood pressure and temperature 4-hourly.
- Do urine dipstick.
- Check fetal heart rate.		- DO NOT perform digital vaginal examination.
- Refer to health centre or hospital.		- If term, this may indicate onset of labour.
- Assess for other signs of labour.
- Perform a sterile speculum examination to assess whether the cervix is open.
- Give antibiotics if prolonged rupture of membranes.
- Allow to deliver if in labour.
Preterm PROM (PPROM)- Assess as indicated in PROM.
- Ultrasound at least twice a day.
- Consider weekly maternal FBC.		- DO NOT perform digital vaginal examination.
- Refer to health centre or hospital.		If rupture is:
- Before 28 weeks: observe vital signs; initiate the process of evacuation by stimulation after counselling the mother and significant others about the risks.
- Before 34 weeks (28–33 weeks): administer steroids – intramuscular betamethasone 12 mg every 12 hours for 24 hours, OR intramuscular dexamethasone.
- Regularly inspect the sanitary pad for the amount, colour and odour of the amniotic fluid.
- Strict bed rest.
- Oral erythromycin and amoxicillin (500 mg PO 6-hourly) should be given for 10 days following the diagnosis of PPROM.
PPROM >34 and <37 weeks, and PROM >37 weeksAssess as indicated in PROM.Refer to hospital (transfer is preferable while the baby is in utero).- Give antibiotic prophylaxis within 8 hours.
- Give steroids before 37 weeks.
- If no evidence of fetal distress, leave the patient for up to 24 hours.
- If the patient does not go into labour within 24 hours, induce.
- Monitor labour normally.

Anaemia in pregnancy by haemoglobin: no anaemia (>11 g/dl), moderate (7-11 g/dl: double-dose iron 3 months), severe (<7 g/dl: urgent referral) – clinic vs hospital management.
>11 g/dl (no pallor): Diagnosis: No clinical anaemia; Clinic / PHU / Health centre and hospital: Give the usual daily dose of iron and folic acid and counsel on compliance. Provide counselling on nutrition.
7–11 g/dl OR palmar and conjunctival pallor: Diagnosis: Moderate anaemia; Clinic / PHU: Give a double dose of daily iron for 3 months and counsel on compliance and nutrition (such as chuchuza, imbuya, spinach etc.); re-assess at the next ANC contact or sooner if danger signs occur. If haemoglobin [<]8 g/dl or symptoms occur (shortness of breath, dizziness), urgently refer to health centre or hospital; Health centre and hospital: Give a double dose of daily iron for 3 months and counsel on compliance and nutrition; re-assess at the next ANC contact or sooner. If symptoms occur, do further clinical and laboratory assessment and treat accordingly.
<7 g/dl and/or severe palmar and conjunctival pallor, OR any pallor with respirations [>]30/minute or breathlessness at rest: Diagnosis: Severe anaemia; Clinic / PHU: Refer urgently to health centre or hospital; Health centre and hospital: Conduct further clinical and laboratory assessment and treat accordingly. Counsel to give birth at a facility with transfusion capacity.

Points to check in the source:
